Issued at 246 PM EST Fri Nov 13 2026

This Afternoon through Tomorrow Night...

Satellite shows an expansive stratus field over the area this 
afternoon, with a few embedded cumulus where showers have developed. 
It's a fairly typical setup given the upper trough which extends 
from the Mississippi valley all the way to the east coast of the US. 
Persistent cold advection within NW flow combined with low cloud 
cover has made for a chilly, blustery day, with most locations in 
the low-to-mid 40s this afternoon. Most of the precipitation which 
has fallen this afternoon has been rain, though there have been 
reports of graupel and/or snow mixing in within the heaviest 
showers. While surface wet-bulb temperatures are in the upper 30s 
and low 40s (unfavorable for frozen precip), llvl lapse rates remain 
steep. ACARS soundings from SDF show observed freezing heights 
around 2600 ft AGL, though saturation within the heaviest showers 
combined with cold air being pulled down to the surface has likely 
supplied just enough cooling for the mixing of wintry p-types. Hi-
res guidance suggests that scattered showers should continue for 
areas mainly east of a Paoli, IN to Tompkinsville, KY line through 
the late evening hours, steadily diminishing in coverage after 
sunset.

The area of richer low-to-mid level moisture will begin to push off 
to the south and east of the area over the next several hours, with 
pockets of clearing observed on satellite over central IN. Would 
expect this area of clearing to grow as we lose daytime heating this 
evening, with a clearing trend from NW to SE expected during the mid-
to-late evening hours. The clearing skies and weakening NW winds 
should allow for more cooling tonight than last night, with forecast 
lows expected to fall into the upper 20s and low 30s by sunrise 
Saturday. 

Something that we'll have to watch for is the development of patchy 
fog, particularly in valleys and areas which receive rain/drizzle 
this afternoon and evening. 12Z REFS guidance shows some potential 
for fog development, and the likelihood of clearing skies and 
residual near-saturated conditions within the BL also support this 
scenario. However, winds will still be around 10 kt at the top of 
the near-sfc inversion layer, so there may be just enough turbulence 
to prevent much fog development. However, any fog which develops 
could lead to slick bridges/overpasses and other elevated surfaces 
Saturday morning given the below freezing temperatures, so extra 
precautions should be taken if traveling early Saturday.

Tomorrow, the upper trough will begin to nudge slightly to the east, 
with sfc high pressure approaching the region from the NW. Residual 
llvl moisture, reinforced by a fetch off of Lake Michigan should 
support the development of stratocu during the day, especially 
across the Bluegrass region. Variations in cloud coverage should 
cause temperatures to vary from NE to SW across the area, with highs 
ranging from the upper 40s in the Bluegrass to the low 50s west of I-
65. Clouds may try to fill in Saturday night from NE to SW, with 
patchy fog possible in areas which stay cloud-free. Low temperatures 
Sunday morning are expected to range from the mid 20s to around 
freezing. 

Sunday through Next Week...

Omega upper ridge pattern sets up across the middle of North America 
for the weekend into early next week as the trough over the eastern 
CONUS continues to gradually move into the Atlantic. Surface high 
pressure will sink toward the Ohio Valley on Sunday, with the heart 
of a cP air mass spreading across the eastern US. The blocked flow 
pattern should support fairly consistent weather conditions from 
Sunday through Tuesday, with the dry air mass (PWAT well below 
0.50"/10th percentile of climo) supporting large diurnal temperature 
swings between sub-freezing lows and highs in the 50s and low 60s.

For the second half of next week, the upper ridge axis will begin to 
shift eastward as troughs eject across the northern Plains and 
central Canada. While these disturbances are not currently expected 
to bring any significant weather to our area, the eroding of the 
upper ridge should allow more warm return flow into the Ohio Valley. 
Above normal temperatures should return by the end of next week, 
with increasing probabilities of high temperatures over 70 Thursday 
into Friday.
